title_original: Stan Douglas and the Photography of What Might Have Been
excerpt_original: He hires extras, builds sets, scans whole crowds through photogrammetry, and out of all of it raises the Gastown riot of 1971 and Penn Station, razed in 1963. The Jeu de Paume gathers some forty of these documentary fictions in the largest exhibition devoted to the Canadian…

blocks.text: Hatted heads crowd the frame. Tweed overcoats. A cigarette burning down in the front row. Hastings Park, 16 July 1955 carries the bite of a press photograph, and the bite is what gives it away: too crisp, too saturated for the year it claims. Stan Douglas, a Vancouver native, speaks of the scene he staged down to the last extra: “The guy on the bottom left is telling off-colour jokes and the woman is clearly offended.” Beneath the smut lies the social anatomy. This racetrack crowd embodies postwar consumerism, “people who were making things being able to buy those things, a sort of perpetual motion machine for capitalism.”

Vancouver has been his laboratory for forty years, its institutional failures his raw material. Abbott & Cordova, 7 August 1971 restages the Gastown riot as nocturnal choreography of an almost indecent beauty: streetlamps, red bodywork, bodies strewn across wet asphalt. Hippies were squatting the warehouses then, to the displeasure of a police force that, as the artist tells it, “would rather keep the communities quarantined.” The print mounts the riot squad’s charge and declines to take sides: “It’s basically there, installed in that location, so you can observe, wonder what happened to this place, and start a conversation.”

Breakdown holds him more than catastrophe. “Typically in almost all of my work, I’m looking at conditions where something has broken down,” he says. “These events, these ruptures, these breakings of habits, are times in which possibilities are found.” Now and then he takes the idea at its word. “Scenes from the Blackout” imagines what a photographer might have caught while the power failures held New York still. In Solitaire , a woman sits on the bare boards of an elevator shaft, an oil lamp her only light.

blocks.text: Thwarted promises come next. “Disco Angola” binds the broke New York of the early 1970s, where dancing passed for escape, to a freshly decolonized Angola. In Two Friends, 1975 , a woman in coral and a man in mint green pose among a club’s gilt moldings, beautiful and already in mourning. The picture carries the gloss of a fashion editorial, and the gloss is the point. Lodged inside it are two confiscated freedoms: disco swallowed by the market, Angolan independence ground down by the Cold War. “Utopias may not last long,” he allows. “But what remains is a model of how a positive future could have taken place.”

Then the means swell. “2011 ≠ 1848” rebuilds the uprisings of Tunis, Hackney, and the Brooklyn Bridge out of press archives and social media. “Penn Station’s Half Century” raises the station razed in 1963 in a light only computer-generated imagery can furnish. A single obsession drives the whole enterprise: “Almost all of the works address moments when history could have gone one way or another. We live in the residue of such moments.” In an age of generative images, such virtuosity unsettles. What it lays bare is how long photography has been arranging the world, and how openly Stan Douglas does his arranging.

blocks.text: An entire gallery belongs to Birth of a Nation , shown in France for the first time. The installation takes apart the chase sequence from D.W. Griffith’s film, the racist epic that single-handedly revived the Ku Klux Klan. Douglas follows the bloodline and finds the descendants where nobody thinks to look: “Mickey, for example, has a black body, wears white gloves and like Jim Crow is prone to convulsive movements that mix the cruelty of his stereotype with laughter.”

Five screens share one wall. Griffith holds the center, ringed by four new vantage points, among them two invented characters whom young Flora collapses into a single terror. The sequence mesmerizes exactly as the original did, then withdraws the pleasure. The hanging turns to color, the rope drops against a blue screen, the actor’s feet find the floor of a present-day studio. The frame widens. A crew member walks a horse toward the wide door, opens it, and goes out into the light. The air comes in.
